wrong_text: Satin weave — the weft floats over four or more warp threads before going under one.
problem: Standard satin weave is warp-faced: it is the WARP yarns that float over multiple weft threads, not the weft over the warp. The weft-over-warp version is sateen (the cotton variant). Describing satin as 'weft floats' reverses the structure and will mislead students in exam answers.
correction: Satin weave — the warp floats over four or more weft threads before going under one. These long warp floats reflect light to create a smooth, lustrous surface.

wrong_text: A satin weave creates a lustrous surface because the weft _____ over four or more warp threads before going under one. [Answer: floats]
problem: Same warp/weft reversal as in content_html. The KC reinforces the incorrect description: in standard satin it is the warp that floats over the weft, not the weft over the warp.
correction: A satin weave creates a lustrous surface because the warp _____ over four or more weft threads before going under one. [Answer: floats]

wrong_text: Why does satin-weave fabric have a lustrous surface? — Long weft floats over four or more warp threads reflect light, creating a smooth, shiny appearance.
problem: Same warp/weft reversal. Flashcard answer incorrectly states weft floats; should be warp floats.
correction: Why does satin-weave fabric have a lustrous surface? — Long warp floats over four or more weft threads reflect light, creating a smooth, shiny appearance.

wrong_text: The membrane contains billions of microscopic pores per square centimetre
problem: The Gore-Tex membrane contains approximately 1.4 billion pores per square centimetre (equivalent to 9 billion per square inch). Saying 'billions' (plural) implies 2 billion or more per cm², which overstates the figure. The correct description is 'over a billion' or 'around 1.4 billion'.
correction: The membrane contains over 1.4 billion microscopic pores per square centimetre

wrong_text: capable of stretching to five to eight times its original length
problem: Multiple technical sources cite elastane stretch at 500–800% of original length (i.e. up to 8× its length, meaning it extends to 8 times its resting dimension). The figure of 'five to eight times' (500–800%) is at the high end of reported ranges; the most commonly cited laboratory figure is around 500–600% (5–6×). The upper bound of '8×' is cited by some sources but is not the standard GCSE-level claim. Low risk of exam error but worth noting the range is wider than typical teaching references.
correction: capable of stretching to five to seven times its original length and recovering fully (some sources cite up to 8×; 5–6× is the most commonly cited figure)
